deck: 20 Head First Java::09 Life and Death of an Object

cards.front: Where do objects live, and where do local variables live?
cards.back: Objects on the heap; locals on the stack
cards.extra: The heap is shared and garbage-collected; the stack is per thread and method-scoped. That split explains both why objects outlive methods and why locals disappear with them.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::07 Variables and Scopes
cards.example:
class HeapDemo { int x; }
class Ex { HeapDemo h = new HeapDemo();   // object on the heap
  { int local = 7;   // local on the stack
    System.out.println(h.x + local); } }

cards.front: How long does an instance variable live?
cards.back: As long as its object does
cards.extra: It sits inside the object on the heap, so it survives every method call on that object and dies only when the object is collected.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::07 Variables and Scopes
cards.example:
class Box { int value = 1; }
class Ex { { Box b = new Box(); System.out.println(b.value); } }   // the instance variable lives with its object

cards.front: How long does a local variable live, and where is it visible?
cards.back: Only while its method is on the stack, and only inside that method
cards.extra: Another method cannot see it, even in the same class — sleep() cannot read a variable declared in read(). That is scope, and it follows the frame.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::07 Variables and Scopes
cards.example:
class Demo {
  static void f() { int local = 7; System.out.println(local); }   // visible only inside f, only while f is on the stack
}
// System.out.println(local);   // compile error outside the method

cards.front: What distinguishes a constructor from a method?
cards.back: Same name as the class and no return type
cards.extra: Writing void Duck() creates an ordinary method that never runs at construction. The missing return type is the signal the compiler looks for.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class Named {
  Named() { }   // same name as the class, no return type: a constructor
  void Named() { }   // with a return type it is just a method
}

cards.front: When does the compiler supply a default no-arg constructor?
cards.back: Only when you declare no constructor at all
cards.extra: Write one constructor and the free no-arg one is gone. That is why adding Duck(int size) breaks every new Duck() in the codebase.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class NoCtor { }
class HasCtor { HasCtor(int x) { } }
class Ex { { NoCtor a = new NoCtor(); } }   // compiler-supplied no-arg constructor
// new HasCtor();   // compile error: none supplied once a constructor exists

cards.front: You wrote only Duck(int size). Does new Duck() compile?
cards.back: No — you must add a no-arg constructor yourself
cards.extra: The compiler only fills in a constructor when the class declares none. This is one of the most common breaking changes when a class gains required state.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class Duck { Duck(int size) { } }
class Ex { { Duck d = new Duck(1); } }
// new Duck();   // compile error: add a no-arg constructor yourself

cards.front: How do you call a superclass constructor from a subclass?
cards.extra: Calling Animal() is illegal — it looks like a method call and will not compile. super is the only route to the parent's constructor.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class Parent { Parent() { } Parent(int x) { } }
class Child extends Parent {
  Child() { super(); }
  Child(int x) { super(x); }
}

cards.front: Why must super() be the first statement in a constructor?
cards.back: The superclass part of the object must be built before the subclass part initialises
cards.extra: Until the parent's fields exist there is nothing for the subclass constructor to rely on. The compiler inserts the call automatically when you omit it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class Base { Base() { System.out.println("base"); } }
class Child extends Base { Child() { super(); System.out.println("child"); } }   // super() first
class Ex { { new Child(); } }   // base part before subclass part

cards.front: What does Java do instead of letting you destroy an object?
cards.back: You abandon it by dropping the last reference; the GC reclaims it
cards.extra: There is no free() or delete. Once an object is eligible the collector may destroy it at any time — and gives no notification when it does.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class Thing { }
class Ex { { Thing t = new Thing(); t = null; } }   // abandon it: the GC reclaims it

cards.front: An object holds more than its own declared fields. What else is in it?
cards.back: The instance variables of every superclass up the inheritance tree
cards.extra: This is why a private field in the parent still occupies space in the child object, and why the parent's methods can read it through the child.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class A { int a = 1; }
class B extends A { int b = 2; }
class Ex { B obj = new B(); { System.out.println(obj.a + " " + obj.b); } }   // A's field and B's field

cards.front: Can a class have more than one constructor?
cards.back: Yes — constructors can be overloaded by parameter list
cards.extra: Two constructors with different parameters are both legal, and new picks one. That is how a class offers both Duck() and Duck(int size).
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class Duck { int size; Duck() { this(1); } Duck(int size) { this.size = size; } }
class Ex { { System.out.println(new Duck().size + " " + new Duck(2).size); } }   // overloaded constructors

cards.front: What does new actually do, step by step?
cards.back: Allocates heap space for the object (including every superclass's fields), then runs a constructor
cards.extra: Object creation is allocation plus initialisation. Fields get their defaults first, then the constructor chain runs from Object down to your class.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class Base { int baseField; }
class Sub extends Base { int subField; Sub() { System.out.println("ctor"); } }
class Ex { { Sub s = new Sub(); } }   // heap space for both fields, then the constructor

cards.front: A method creates an object, keeps it in a local variable, and returns. What happens to the object?
cards.back: It becomes eligible for GC — the only reference died with the stack frame
cards.extra: The object is still on the heap, but nothing can reach it now. The collector may reclaim it at any point, or not until memory is needed.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::07 Object Lifecycle
cards.example:
class Maker { static void make() { Object o = new Object(); } }   // reference dies with the stack frame
class Ex { { Maker.make(); } }   // object now eligible for GC
